_comment: Curriculum roadmap for the daily 'new unit' scheduled task. Every run, the task builds ONE new unit for EACH of the 6 CEFR levels (not a rotation anymore). Each level's 'queue' is an ordered list of not-yet-built units — the task pops the first item off each level's queue, builds it, removes it from that queue, and bumps that level's nextUnitNumber. If a level's queue is empty on a given day, that level is skipped for the day (noted in the run summary) while the other levels still get built. If ALL 6 queues are empty, set _needsMoreRoadmap to true and stop. From 2026-07-11 onward, this roadmap is grounded in the site owner's own teaching decks (uploaded: Adv/Disadv, Cause & Solution, Direct Question, and Opinion essay guides for Task 2; Bar Chart, Line Graph, Pie Chart, Table, Process/Diagram, and Map decks for Task 1). It systematically walks students through her real essay taxonomy (Opinion/Agree-Disagree; Advantages & Disadvantages in its two forms — no-opinion vs 'do advantages outweigh disadvantages'; Cause-Solution in its three often-confused forms — Solution Essay, Cause-Solution Essay, Problem-Solution Essay; and Direct Question in its four forms by number of questions asked) and her real Task 1 chart taxonomy (bar, line, pie, table, process/diagram cycle vs man-made process, and map with its tense rules), each introduced at the CEFR level where its complexity fits, using her actual structural rules (intro-overview-body paragraphing, word count targets, grouping/selectivity rules for tables, tense rules for maps, pie-chart phrase bank, etc.).

queue.title: One Stage of a Process
queue.notes: Write one simple sentence naming a single stage of a short process (e.g. a simplified book-publishing step), bridging the existing A1 'first/next/finally' pattern toward Task 1 process diagrams.

queue.title: Yes or No, One Reason
queue.notes: Answer a simple yes/no direct question with one opinion sentence plus one reason, distinguishing a Direct Question response from a full opinion-essay paragraph.

queue.title: What Happens Next? (Two-Step Process)
queue.notes: Describe two stages of a simplified process (e.g. applying for a study visa) using 'then' and 'after that', a stepping stone toward full first/next/finally sequencing already covered at B1.

queue.title: Positive or Negative? One Paragraph
queue.notes: Answer a 'positive or negative development' direct question (the real Direct Question Essay Type 2) with an opinion and one reason.

queue.title: Positive or Negative Development (Full)
queue.notes: Answer a 'positive or negative development' direct question in a full paragraph with a clear stance and supporting reason, matching real Direct Question Essay Type 2.

queue.title: A Cycle in Order
queue.notes: Describe a natural cycle (not a man-made process) using sequencing language, introducing the real distinction between the two process-diagram subtypes: cycles vs man-made processes.

queue.title: Cause, Then Solution
queue.notes: Answer both parts of a real Cause-Solution prompt (e.g. rising urban populations): state the causes of a problem, then propose solutions, keeping the two clearly separate as the deck instructs.

queue.title: Table Report: Grouping Small Numbers
queue.notes: Practice grouping several small percentages into one summarising phrase instead of listing each one, and singling out any unusually high figure, per the real table-strategy deck.

queue.title: Two Questions: Reasons and Opinion
queue.notes: Answer a real two-question Direct Question prompt — first the reasons behind a trend, then your opinion on it — keeping the two answers clearly separate, matching Direct Question Essay Type 3.

queue.title: A Man-Made Process, Passive Voice
queue.notes: Describe a manufacturing-style process using the passive voice throughout, distinguishing this real process subtype from the natural-cycle subtype covered at B1.

queue.title: Full Table Report: Selectivity Under Pressure
queue.notes: Write a complete table report demonstrating selective grouping and avoidance of over-paraphrasing, per the real table deck's warning against 'risky paraphrasing' (changing words you're not confident about).

queue.title: Advantages, Disadvantages, and a Verdict
queue.notes: Write a complete advantages-disadvantages paragraph that both weighs which side is stronger (Type 2) and closes with a clearly justified verdict, synthesising both real essay subtypes into one response.
